speaker_role: current admissions officer (Harvard College), official office channel
key_insights: Applications that stand out let the reader truly get to know the applicant; forcing yourself into a presumed ideal box makes them feel generic.
Personality should come through in essays, the supplement, the activities grid and any alumni interview.
On AP vs IB vs dual enrollment, the office does not prescribe; it turns the question back to applicants to pick the most challenging path they can succeed in.
Stay organized with a tracking system for deadlines and requirements, and give teachers and counselors ample lead time for recommendations.
Confirm each school actually offers programs matching your interests before applying.
Harvard describes financial aid as need-based and points families to its net price calculator.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Restrictive early action deadline November 1; decisions mid-December; nonbinding but no other private early applications (officer).
Regular decision deadline January 1; outcomes by April 1; reply by May 1 (officer).
Supplement has five short-answer questions; testing, transcript and recommendation letters required (officer).
About 50 fields of study; students choose after three semesters; 96% graduation rate; nearly all live on campus four years (officer).
Officer claims Harvard is cheaper than the local state university for 90% of American families.
notable_or_distinctive: Direct official statement of timelines, requirements and the refusal to recommend a specific course track.
reliability_notes: Official but promotional and about two years old; deadlines, testing requirements and cost claims should be re-checked.
